title: Chapter 171 – The Seventh Door
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

They find the way on the fourth morning after the shed, and it is exactly where Cheng Hui said it would be, which he finds almost insulting.

"It is in plain sight," he says, standing at the foot of the black granite in the cold blue corridor with his lamp held up. "I walked past it a dozen times. I read the inscription. I measured the stone. And I did not once think to ask why a cornerstone, which is by definition the lowest and most solid thing in a building, should have a hollow sound."

"You tapped it?" says Jian.

"Yesterday. With the pommel of Duan Ke's sword." The scholar sniffs. "He was not pleased."

"I was not," says Duan Ke, from the shadows.

Jian leans on his staff and looks at the stone. It stands in its niche as before, tall as a man and half as wide, with its band of spiky characters and its ring of nine small circles: eight polished, one scored through. The air at its foot is cold. There is a faint thin whistle in the dark, so quiet he thought at first it was his own breath.

Yue is already kneeling in front of it. She has her palm against the ninth circle, the scratched one, and her eyes are closed, and her face has the faint, listening stillness that he has learned to watch for. After a long moment she opens her eyes. She takes up the slate.

It's not a stone, she writes. It's a lid.

"A lid?"

There's air behind it. Moving. And it is humming. Not like the Gate. Slower. Like something breathing in its sleep.

Jian looks at the circles. He thinks of the table, and the nine chairs, and a voice saying consent of the Nine.

"Then I think," he says, "we know what the circles are for."

* * *

Cheng Hui explains the stone over breakfast, with a piece of burnt toast in one hand and an air of intense and private triumph.

"It was the whistling," he says. "Yue noticed it first. She felt it in the floor, and told me, and I thought it was draft. But a draft does not whistle in a rhythm. This one rose and fell, rose and fell, with a period of eleven seconds." He taps the toast on the table. "That is not wind. That is breathing."

"Whose?" Bell asks.

"I did not know. I still do not." His eyes gleam. "But I traced it to the cornerstone, and I traced the cornerstone's measurements against Mr. Cole's notes, and the notes mention, in three places, a thing he calls the keeper's gate. A door for the holders of the Nine. A way for them to visit each other, in the early days, when the Doors were new."

"A tunnel."

"A road." He smiles. "And roads, madam, go somewhere."

Duan Ke, across the table, has a mouthful of rice and an expression of deep skepticism. "You worked all that out from a whistle."

"I worked it out from a whistle, a diary, a diagram, and the fact that the Nine were obsessively tidy." Cheng Hui spreads his hands. "A scholar is a person who has learned to notice when something is too neat."

Yue holds up her slate. I noticed the whistle first.

"You did," says the scholar, bowing. "And I am deeply in your debt."

She looks pleased. Beside her, Mo Yan is trying to feed toast to a patient and unimpressed Ao.

* * *

They say their farewells at the bridge, the night before.

It is not planned. They go down in ones and twos, the children first, with Nurse leading them across the humming black span like ducklings. Jian waits at the head of the stair with the staff in his hand, and watches them go, and does not follow. He has said goodbye to many people in his life. He has never learned how.

When he finally crosses, the platform is full. Ao is on the cushions with his head against the glass, whispering to a small bead of light in a thin man's hands. Tao stands stiffly beside him with his top, scowling, not saying a word. Mo Yan has drawn a picture on the crystal with her charcoal: nine figures in a ring round a tree, and a tiny tenth figure at the edge, with a crown of light.

Ethan Cole sits with his face lifted and his eyes shut. There is a smile on it. It is the first Jian has seen that did not look like a wound.

They've been telling me about the table, he says, without opening his eyes. All of it. The vote. The tea. The rice cakes. I wish I'd been there.

"You were there," says Jian. "Through the wall."

So I was. The smile deepens. It wasn't the same.

Mei's voice is a bead of silver, very quiet. They're going, Papa.

I know.

It's all right.

I know it is. The old man's hands tremble, and steady. I'm going to be very bad at this. I want you to know that. I'm going to cry for at least a week.

That's all right, too.

Nurse is the last to speak. She stands at the lip of the bridge, as she has stood for six hundred years, with her hands folded in front of her and her eyes bright. She does not say goodbye. She says, "Go home." And Jian bows to her, very low, as he would to his mother, and turns and walks away without looking back.

* * *

It takes all of them.

They stand in a half circle at the foot of the stone: eight children, if one can call them that, and the old man with the staff. The seven Operators who are awake, and the eighth, the key, the one who walks. They have drawn lots for the circles and then discarded the lots, because Cheng Hui pointed out that the circles were numbered, and that the numbers corresponded, in the old script, to the Operators' own.

Ao stands at the first. Cheng Hui at the second. Duan Ke at the third. Hai Ren at the fourth, long-fingered, serene. Zhen Li at the fifth, with his brass lantern at his feet and his small face blank and bright. Mo Yan at the sixth, with her charcoal clenched in her teeth. Tao at the seventh, nose almost level with the stone.

Jian stands at the eighth.

The ninth is left. The scratched one. Nobody has been told what to do about it.

"I do not like this," Bell murmurs, from the back. "I do not like any of this."

"I know."

"If the stone is a trap—"

"It is not a trap. It is a vow." He keeps his voice low. "I think it was made to be opened by the ones who would not dare to open it. A door that can only be unlocked by consent. It is the kindest lock I have ever seen."

She makes a skeptical sound. But she does not move.

Cheng Hui looks round the half circle. "On my word," he says. "Place your hands on the circle and say, aloud, that you consent. Nothing more. I do not know whether it will work. I only know it is what the stone asks."

"What about the ninth?" asks Tao.

From the corridor behind them, through the little brass grille set high in the wall, a thin voice says, I'll do it.

Everyone turns.

I can't reach, says Mei. Papa's carrying me. But I can say it from here. If somebody will put a hand on the scratch.

Yue is already moving. She crosses the floor with her red cloak swinging and lays her palm flat on the ninth circle. She looks up at the grille and nods.

Then, says Mei, I consent.

* * *

The stone does not open. It sings.

It is a low, rising chord, eight notes laid on one another, and a ninth that is not a note at all but a silence shaped like one. The black granite shivers. A thin line of white light runs down the middle of the face, from the top to the base, and the two halves of the stone, smoothly and without a sound, slide apart.

Behind them is a corridor.

It is narrow, and straight, and not of the Hall. The walls are rough-hewn, the color of old bone, scored with fine lines like the grain of ancient wood. The floor is bare stone worn smooth in the center by the passage of feet. There is a smell: dust, and iron, and something older that Jian cannot name. A pale steel-blue light rises from a seam along the ceiling and runs away into the distance, thin as a thread.

At the far end, small with distance, a door stands waiting.

It is tall, and black, and edged with white fire.

"Door Seven," whispers Cheng Hui.

Nobody moves. Ao has crept up against Jian's leg and put his hand in Jian's, and Jian closes his fingers round it. Somewhere ahead, in the blue-lit dark, something is breathing: a slow, deep, patient breath, as of a sleeper dreaming of a hill.

Jian takes a step forward. His staff taps on the stone. He feels, as he does so, the old tightness in his chest, and the weariness in his knees, and the soft pulse of the panel waiting at the edge of his sight. None of them matter. There is a door at the end of a long blue corridor, and something behind it that breathes.

"Wait here," he says.

"No," says Bell.

"Bell—"

"No. We go together. You have said it yourself." Her chin is up. "We do not do things alone anymore."

He looks at her, and at the line of faces, and at the black door in the distance. Then, slowly, he nods.

"Together," he says.

* * *

The corridor is longer than it looks.

They walk for a quarter of an hour. The passage does not bend or branch. The blue light flickers on the walls, and their footsteps echo, and the breathing grows louder with every step, until Jian can feel it in his teeth. Duan Ke goes first, with the pale blade drawn. Hai Ren walks beside him, hands folded. Behind them come the others in a loose procession, the little ones in the middle, Yue and Bell guarding the rear.

The door grows.

When they reach it, Jian has to tilt his head back to see the top. It is twenty feet tall, and as black as a lacquer bowl, with a surface so smooth that the lamplight slides off it. The white seam round the edge is not light, he sees, but a crack: a narrow, glowing, fissure-thin line where the door meets the frame. Heat rolls out of it. Heat, and a sound he has been hearing all along without placing it.

It is the sound of a very large thing, on the other side, breathing.

A bench stands to one side of the door. It is a plain wooden bench, worn and pale, the sort of thing one finds in a country inn. On the bench sits a young man.

He is nineteen. Thin, quick, narrow-faced, with a shock of untidy black hair and a mouth that quirks at one corner as though he has just heard a joke he does not intend to share. He wears a plain brown tunic and soft boots. His hands are folded round one knee. His outline is faintly silver, as if lit from within, and through his chest, dim and ghostly, Jian can see the black of the door.

He lifts his head, and looks at them, and his eyes are the brightest thing in the corridor.

"You're early," says Kito.

* * *

Nobody says anything. Jian is not sure that anyone is breathing.

"I'm sorry." The young man swings his legs off the bench and stands. He is shorter than Jian expected. "That was rude. I've been rehearsing a better opening for about four hundred years and I can't remember a word of it. Hello. I'm Kito. I hold the Seventh Door." He glances over the line of faces and his smile widens, crooked and warm. "You must be the Operators. Look at you! All of you! You're so small."

"We are not," says Duan Ke, stiffly.

"Of course not. I meant it affectionately." Kito bows, a little awkwardly. "And you must be the Eighth. The one who walked. I've been looking forward to meeting you. Ethan wrote me a very long letter about you, and I'm afraid I read it eleven times."

Jian's mouth is dry. "A letter."

"In the sixth year. Before he sealed himself in the well." Kito's eyes dance. "He said you'd be stubborn and kind and terribly tired. He said I'd know you by your staff. I'd like to say I recognized you, but I've never been good with faces. I'm better with the future."

"You are a seer," says Cheng Hui.

"I'm a stored seer. It's not the same. I can't see past the day I died, and that was nineteen years old and four hundred years ago." Kito's laugh is light. "But I have been thinking, in the meantime. About what I'd say. And I'm afraid it's not what you hoped."

Jian feels the cold settle in his chest. "What do you mean?"

The young man sits back down on the bench. He looks, for a moment, a great deal older.

"You think I'm a door," he says. "A passage. A shortcut home."

"We had hoped—"

"I know. It's what Ethan hoped, too. It's what the Nine intended, in the beginning." His expression is gentle. "But the tunnel was never meant to carry you. It was meant to carry them."

* * *

Kito, it turns out, cannot resist the children.

He hears Ao's stifled giggle from behind Jian's leg, and his whole face changes. He drops to a crouch with a wave of his silver hand and says, in a conspiratorial whisper, "I can see you, you know. You're hiding behind the tall one."

Ao peeps out. He has the rabbit under his chin. "Are you a ghost?"

"Partly."

"Does it hurt?"

"Being a ghost?" Kito considers. "Mostly it's boring. You sit on a bench. Nobody visits. You count the cracks in the ceiling, and then you count them again." He leans in. "There are four hundred and twelve. I'll tell you which is my favorite later."

"Which one?"

"The one shaped like a duck."

Ao gasps. "I like ducks!"

"Everyone does. It's a deeply underrated animal." Kito rises, holding out a hand, and Ao takes it with the solemn gravity of a general accepting a sword. The silver fingers do not pass through him. They close, gently, round the small hand.

Mo Yan is at his elbow in a moment, tugging at his tunic. When he looks down she holds up her charcoal and her sheet of paper, and he laughs.

"You want to draw me? I'd be flattered. I've never sat for a portrait." He settles on the bench, hands round one knee, and lifts his chin. "Make me handsome, please. It's for posterity."

Mo Yan draws. Her tongue pokes out. Her hand flies. In a minute she turns the sheet round, and Kito looks at it for a long time without a word.

It is a boy of nineteen, sitting on a bench with a crooked grin, and over his shoulder, small and bright, the faint shape of a tree.

"That," he says at last, hoarsely, "is the nicest thing anyone has done for me in four hundred years."

Mo Yan puts her charcoal behind her ear and nods, as if it were nothing at all.

* * *

He tells it standing, with his hands flat on the black door.

"The Sixth Door is a hall of the sick," he says. "Two hundred thousand, give or take. People who needed rest. People who were dying of the world. That's what you've been living in. A very large and very kind infirmary." He looks over his shoulder. "This is the other thing."

He presses his palm against the door. The white seam flares.

"The Rest of All," says Kito, "is behind me."

Jian's mind goes blank.

"All of it. Every one of the others. The people we reached. The ones who said yes. We put them under the valley, under the roots, in a hall that makes the one above you look like a closet." The young man's voice drops. "Nine million, four hundred thousand."

Nobody moves. The breathing behind the door rises and falls.

"That's what I hold," Kito says. "That's what the tree is for. That's what Ethan's daughter was never told. The Sixth Door was where he put the girl. This is where the world is sleeping."

"Nine million," whispers Cheng Hui. His face has gone the color of chalk.

"And four hundred thousand." Kito's grin is brittle. "The extra four hundred thousand are the ones I like best."

Jian leans on his staff. The floor tilts a little. In his chest the boy has gone entirely silent, and he can hear, faintly, the stove ticking in the small round room.

"And the beasts?" he says.

"Are not coming for the Hall." Kito's eyes meet his. "They never were. The Hall was bait. The crawlers are scouts. The Seam knows where the sleepers are, and it has known for four hundred years. But it could not reach them while the Doors held." The young man's voice cracks. "And then the Sixth began to fail."

* * *

"It was the shed," Kito says.

He says it quietly, without cruelty, and Jian feels it like a knife.

"The Hall's failure was already weakening the Seam's hold. But a Door that sheds is a Door that dies, and the Seam can feel it. Twenty-two thousand lights went out in a night. Thirty thousand with the eighth. Every one was a break in the pattern." He rubs his face with a silver hand. "I felt it from here. Four hundred miles. It was like hearing a bell crack."

Bell's voice is hoarse. "You are saying the beasts came because of the shed?"

"I'm saying the tide was supposed to come in sixty days. Ao was right. That's what the old figures said." His smile is bleak. "It's nine, now. Nine days to the Wall. Perhaps ten, if the weather holds."

"Nine," says Jian.

"The beasts that came to the Hall were a distraction. The real tide is rising under the valley." He looks at Jian, and for the first time the brightness in his face dims. "It's going to hit the Wall, and then the village, and then the roots. And if it reaches the roots, there is nothing I can do."

The silence is absolute. Ao's hand tightens in Jian's.

"Nine days," says Jian again. "It took us a hundred and nineteen years to walk here."

"I know."

"We cannot possibly—"

"There is a way." Kito raises a silver hand. "I told you. I'm not what you hoped. But I'm not nothing, either."

* * *

The way is simple. It is also terrible.

"The tunnel runs four hundred miles," says Kito. "From this door to the roots. It's the Nine's last road. It's straight, and level, and wide enough for a cart. On foot it takes seven days. At a run, if you do not stop, perhaps five." He folds his hands. "That's not enough. Not with children."

"The Core Step—" begins Jian.

"Is a stride across the world's skin. This is under it. You cannot fold the ground you're standing on." Kito shakes his head. "But there's another way. A door can fold the road if the Nine consent. It's what the circles were for. A passage, not a step. It would carry all of you, all nine, to the other end in a single night."

"And the cost?" says Cheng Hui, softly.

"Ah." The young man's eyes slide away. "That's the part I like least."

He is silent for a moment.

"A fold costs the one who holds the door," he says. "That's always been the rule. Whoever stands in the gap. The Nine built the Doors so that the holder would be spent, over time, a little at each use. I've been spent for four hundred years." A faint smile. "I'm not very much left."

Jian understands before the others do. He feels the knowledge arrive, calm and cold, like a stone settling to the bottom of a well.

"You," he says.

"I'm a stored mind, Lin Jian. I have what I have. A fold to the roots costs more than I've got." Kito spreads his hands. "It would use me up. All of me. I would go out like a lamp."

Bell makes a small broken sound.

"And the Seventh Door would open," says Cheng Hui, slowly. "From the valley side. When the tree fruits."

"It's the only way to open it. The holder has to be gone."

"And if you do not do it?"

"Then you walk seven days, and arrive on the tenth, and the Wall is already down." The young man shrugs. "That's the choice. A boy of nineteen, who has been dead for four hundred years. Or the village."

Jian says "No" before the young man has finished.

He does not remember deciding. The word is out of his mouth the moment the silver hand lifts toward the black door, and he takes a step forward, and the staff rings on the stone. "No. Kito. Stop."

The young man glances round. He is still smiling. "I haven't started."

"I will not allow it."

"It isn't yours to allow." Kito's voice is gentle. "I'm the holder. The door is mine. The cost is mine. And I've been waiting four hundred years to spend it on something that matters."

"You are nineteen."

"I was nineteen. I'm a good deal older now." The bright eyes soften. "Look. I know what you're thinking. You've done this before. You've stood in front of someone who was about to give themselves up, and you've said no, and they've listened, because you're the sort of man people listen to. And you've watched them live, and you've thought, good, that's how it should be."

Jian does not answer.

"But I'm a seer. I can see how it goes. If I don't do this, you walk seven days and arrive late. The Wall falls. Your mother is in the valley. Your sister is in the valley. The man who taught you to fight is on the Wall." Kito's voice is quiet. "I've seen the end of it, Lin Jian. I won't tell you what it looks like."

"You said you can't see past your own death."

"I can see around it." A flicker of the old humor. "That's more than most."

Jian stares at him. His throat is tight and his eyes burn. Beside him Bell has taken his arm, and he can feel her trembling.

Brother, says the boy, in the small round room. He's not scared.

I know.

How can he not be scared?

I do not know. Jian's voice is a whisper. Perhaps because he has had a long time to practice.

* * *

The corridor is very quiet.

Kito looks at Jian for a long moment, and then, to everyone's astonishment, he laughs. It is a soft, helpless, delighted laugh, and it rings off the bone-pale walls.

"You really do look like him," he says. "I'd forgotten how much." He wipes his eye with a silver knuckle. "All right. I'll tell you what I tell everyone. You can hate me for it later."

"Kito—"

"I'm the seer. I already know how it ends." He lifts one hand, and the white seam of the door flares. "Tell the girl the joke wasn't that bad."

And he turns, and lays both palms flat on the black door.
